newsitem.title: POLAND: Ending visas with Russia won't boost crime-Poland.
newsitem.headline: Ending visas with Russia won't boost crime-Poland.

text.p: Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said on Friday an agreement with Russia on visa-free travel would make little difference to cross-border criminal gangs.
Cimoszewicz signed the deal with his counterpart, Viktor Chernomyrdin, during a four-day visit.
The agreement, which allows citizens to enter each other's countries without visas, had attracted criticism that it could make it easier for rampant Russian crime gangs to enter Poland.

"We already have problems associated with international crime. Experience shows that for organised crime gangs, whether or not visas are required does not have much significance," Cimoszewicz told reporters at Warsaw airport.
He added that greater ease of contacts was important for the vast majority of ordinary travellers.

The agreement had been delayed because Warsaw insisted that it be tied to another, obliging Russia to re-admit illegal immigrants from third countries who had crossed from its territory into Poland -- a condition rejected by Moscow.

Cimoszewicz said the Russians had now come round, especially after being told that Poland's similar arrangements with Ukraine did not involve large numbers of cases. But as the Russians had not been prepared in advance to sign the readmission deal, the agreement would be concluded shortly and only then would visa-free travel take effect.

Poland hopes to join the European Union soon and EU member states have expressed worries over the control of the flow of crime and illegal immigration across Poland's borders with Belarus, Ukraine and Russia's Kaliningrad region.
Immigrants from various countries are frequently caught crossing westwards into Poland on their way to Germany.
Cimoszewicz said his Russian trip had been extremely successful, adding: "With all my interlocutors I encountered a very friendly attitude and desire to develop relations with Poland."

The two former Warsaw Pact allies disagree over Poland's bid to join NATO, despite Russian fears that expansion of the Western defence alliance might threaten its own security, but they focused on other issues during the visit.

The Polish premier also signed deals in Moscow covering future trade liberalisation and a settlement of communist-era mutual trade debts dating back to the 1980s when the two countries were in the now-defunct Comecon trade bloc.

Cimoszewicz met officials and businessmen in St Petersburg and on Friday visited the Tatarstan autonomous region in central Russia. Poland is interested in importing oil from Tatarstan and exporting manufactured goods.

Polish television said the Tatarstan government had proposed 30 projects for which it would offer financial guarantees to Polish investors in the fields of oil extraction and processing, food production and machinery.
